verdict.reason: A rare theatrical film continuation of Ikuhara's singular vision, essential for understanding how the director transformed his TV series into something stranger and more urgent. The film's aggressive collage style and narrative density demand the immersion of a cinema screen.

ratings.plot: A young man and woman meet on a train in Europe, and wind up spending one evening together in Vienna. Unfortunately, both know that this will probably be their only night together.

verdict.reason: See it for Linklater's real-time dialogue and the way he lets a single night breathe across two hours without manufactured drama. The script trusts conversation itself to carry the entire film, which remains rare and worth experiencing in a theater.

ratings.plot: A young woman who exudes sexuality battles temptation.

verdict.reason: A sharp, funny film about desire and self-sabotage that still cuts deeper than most period dramas made today. Laura Dern's performance is fearless and specific—she finds the intelligence and loneliness underneath all the surface charm.

ratings.plot: A truck driver stops at a small family-run noodle shop and decides to help its fledgling business. The story is intertwined with various vignettes about the relationship of love and food.

verdict.reason: A genuinely funny film about obsession that works as both comedy and food philosophy, worth seeing on a big screen. Itami's ramen-shop narrative wraps around surreal vignettes that land better in a theater than at home, where the absurdist rhythm holds its power.

ratings.plot: In Paris outskirts Blanche, a young clerk, befriends Lea, a girl livelier than she is. Lea is going steady with Fabien who is a friend to Alexandre who is going steady with Adrienne but is however loved by Blanche. Somehow a way h...

verdict.reason: One of Rohmer's finest comedies of remarriage, built on the pleasure of watching four people negotiate desire through conversation and accident. The 103 minutes moves like a Parisian stroll, and the emotional precision of the final act justifies every minute spent watching these characters circle each other.

movies.title: Four Adventures of Reinette and Mirabelle

ratings.plot: Two unlike girls are going to learn each other's world - lovely countryside and bustling Paris.

verdict.reason: Rohmer's most accessible film still rewards close attention to his moral universe. The episodic structure builds to surprising emotional weight.

ratings.plot: A young woman returns to her hometown of Turin to set up a new fashion salon and gets involved with a troubled woman and her three wealthy friends.

verdict.reason: Antonioni's debut feature is a masterclass in visual restraint and emotional precision that demands the theater's full screen. Metrograph's restoration allows you to catch the geometry of each room and the distance between characters as the director intended.

ratings.plot: Autumn Moon (Sam Lee), a low-rent triad living in Hong Kong, struggles to find meaning in his hopelessly violent existence.

verdict.reason: Fruit Chan's debut is essential cinema about triad life in the margins of 1990s Hong Kong, shot with raw urgency on DV before the format became fashionable. The handheld image and Sam Lee's performance capture desperation without sentimentality, making this a rare theatrical opportunity to see where Hong Kong's indie tradition began.

ratings.plot: Documentary filmmaker Ross McElwee sets out to make a movie about Union General Sherman's March to the Sea towards the end of the American Civil War, but keeps getting sidetracked by his own love life.

verdict.reason: One of the great American experimental documentaries deserves to be seen theatrically in its full rambling glory. Ross McElwee's four-hour digression from General Sherman to his own romantic misadventures is a singular work of cinema that only works as a committed sit-down experience.

ratings.plot: Eight-year-old Ahmed has mistakenly taken his friend Mohammad's notebook. He wants to return it, or else his friend will be expelled from school. The boy determinedly sets out to find Mohammad's home in the neighbouring village.

verdict.reason: Kiarostami's breakthrough transforms a simple premise into profound cinema. The Iranian landscape and natural light create images that lose impact on small screens.

ratings.plot: Pulp novelist Holly Martins travels to shadowy, postwar Vienna, only to find himself investigating the mysterious death of an old friend, Harry Lime.

verdict.reason: This is essential cinema—see it on the biggest screen available. Carol Reed's use of Dutch angles and Vienna's bomb-crater geography makes this a film that demands theatrical space.

ratings.plot: Paddington, now happily settled with the Brown family and a popular member of the local community, picks up a series of odd jobs to buy the perfect present for his Aunt Lucy's 100th birthday, only for the gift to be stolen.

verdict.reason: A family film with the visual precision and emotional intelligence of a great animated feature, executed in live action. Paul King's framing, blocking, and color sense elevate every frame beyond what the premise demands.

ratings.plot: Set in early 19th century Romania, a policeman, Costandin, is hired by a nobleman to find a Gypsy slave who has run away from his estate after having an affair with his wife.

verdict.reason: Radu Jude's control of tone across comedy, cruelty, and social critique is flawless—he makes a 19th-century manhunt feel urgent and modern. The black-and-white cinematography and dialect work lock you into a specific historical moment that demands the theatrical image.

ratings.plot: When a litter of Dalmatian puppies are abducted by the minions of Cruella De Vil, the owners must find them before she uses them for a diabolical fashion statement.
ratings.director: Clyde Geronimi, Hamilton Luske, Wolfgang Reitherman

verdict.reason: A foundational Disney film that still works as pure entertainment on the big screen. Cruella remains one of animation's most magnetic villains, and the hand-drawn chase sequences have a kinetic energy that streaming flattens.

ratings.plot: A self-conscious woman juggles adjusting to her new role as an aristocrat's wife and avoiding being intimidated by his first wife's spectral presence.

verdict.reason: Hitchcock's command of Gothic atmosphere and psychological tension makes this essential viewing on the big screen. Joan Fontaine's performance captures the quiet terror of living in a dead woman's shadow with unmatched precision.

movies.title: Marcel the Shell with Shoes On

ratings.plot: A cash-strapped documentary maker decides to make his newest documentary about a mollusk shell he finds living in his Airbnb with his friends.

verdict.reason: A genuinely original film that earns its emotional weight through tiny, precise details and a real voice—see it before word-of-mouth turns it into a meme. Fleischer-Camp's stop-motion work captures something between live-action documentary and animation that feels like nothing else in theaters.

ratings.plot: Three parties and a witness have four versions of a rape/murder in ninth-century Japan.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's essential films about the nature of truth itself—see it on the big screen where Kurosawa's compositions in the forest have maximum impact. The four conflicting accounts of a single crime remain as structurally innovative and philosophically unsettling as they were in 1950.

ratings.plot: The relationship between a father and daughter is complicated by the arrival of a handsome young man.

verdict.reason: Denis makes a masterpiece from stillness and glance—see it on a big screen where the space between characters matters more than the plot. The cinematography transforms an ordinary Paris apartment into a chamber where every look and silence carries weight.

ratings.plot: A counterfeit bill that starts off as a schoolboy prank leads to incarceration and violence.

verdict.reason: Bresson's final film is a masterclass in how cinema conveys moral ruin through gesture and circumstance alone. The 85-minute runtime and stark black-and-white photography make this essential viewing on a theater screen, where every cut and glance carries weight.

ratings.plot: A national manhunt is ordered for a rebellious kid and his foster uncle who go missing in the wild New Zealand bush.

verdict.reason: Waititi finds real warmth in a buddy story that moves at a clip without sacrificing character or humor. The New Zealand bush becomes a third protagonist, and the film knows exactly when to shift from comedy to something tender.

ratings.plot: Cat is a solitary animal, but as its home is devastated by a great flood, he finds refuge on a boat populated by various species, and will have to team up with them despite their differences.

verdict.reason: A visually inventive animated film that justifies the theatrical experience with its fluid watercolor palette and wordless storytelling across a full feature. Zilbalodis uses the absence of dialogue to let image and sound design carry the entire emotional weight, something that needs a theater to land properly.

ratings.plot: On lakeside summer holiday, a conflicted older man is dared to have a flirt with two beautiful teenage half-sisters despite his betrothal to a diplomat's daughter and the fact that the girls have boyfriends.

verdict.reason: Rohmer's greatest work about desire and constraint deserves the big screen. The film unfolds through conversation and gesture with such precision that every moment of restraint feels like an act of will.

ratings.plot: 24 hours in the lives of three young men in the French suburbs the day after a violent riot.

verdict.reason: This is essential cinema about rage, class, and state violence that hasn't aged a day. Kassovitz's black-and-white cinematography and real-time structure make the 98 minutes feel urgent and alive on a big screen.

ratings.plot: This Hong Kong-set crime drama follows the lives of a hitman, hoping to get out of the business, and his elusive female partner.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked Hong Kong comes alive on a big screen where you can catch every detail of his restless camera. The film's kinetic energy gets lost on smaller formats.

ratings.plot: A girl with few real prospects joins a gang, reinventing herself and gaining a sense of self confidence in the process. However, she soon finds that this new life does not necessarily make her any happier.

verdict.reason: Sciamma captures the texture of adolescent reinvention with unflinching clarity and visual precision. Metrograph's 35mm print restores the film's grain and color grading to their intended richness.

ratings.plot: Odysseus, king of Ithaca, embarks on a perilous journey to return home after the Trojan War.

verdict.reason: Nolan shooting on 70mm IMAX demands the largest available screen, and this is the rare theatrical event that justifies the format's expense. Catch it at AMC Lincoln Square 13 or Regal Union Square in 70mm before it vanishes from multiplexes.

ratings.plot: Joe and Angela's marriage is on thin ice. When they invite their enigmatic upstairs neighbors for a dinner party, the night spirals into unexpected places.

verdict.reason: Olivia Wilde directs a sharp ensemble comedy about marriage and desire that lands its tonal shifts without breaking character. The dinner party structure keeps the night contained and tense, letting the cast breathe in ways broader comedies rarely allow.

ratings.plot: A frigid young housewife decides to spend her midweek afternoons as a prostitute.

verdict.reason: Buñuel's masterpiece of desire and repression demands the big screen—the dream sequences and tonal shifts land hardest when you can't pause. This 1967 restoration reveals the precise visual language Buñuel uses to collapse the boundary between fantasy and respectability.

ratings.plot: After his family is murdered by a notorious and ruthless bandit, a former police officer enlists the services of two outlaws to capture the bandit.

verdict.reason: One of the greatest action films ever made—see it on a big screen where the landscapes, stunts, and melodrama hit with full force. At 162 minutes, this 1975 Ramesh Sippy film demands theatrical commitment, and the restoration prints circulating now reveal detail that streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: While a zombie virus breaks out in South Korea, passengers struggle to survive on the train from Seoul to Busan.

verdict.reason: A rare action-horror film that executes both genres with precision and genuine emotional stakes. Yeon Sang-ho's direction of the confined train setting creates escalating tension that justifies the two-hour runtime.

ratings.plot: A documentary about writer and director Brian De Palma.

verdict.reason: Essential viewing for anyone serious about cinema craft and narrative design. Baumbach and Paltrow let De Palma himself do the teaching, breaking down how he builds suspense and composes a frame with the precision of a surgeon.

ratings.plot: Two boys begin a silence strike to press their parents into buying them a television set.

verdict.reason: One of Ozu's masterpieces about Japanese family life, rendered in color for the first time in this restoration. The deadpan humor and formal compositions make this a rare theatrical event that demands a big screen.

ratings.plot: After breaking the mysterious "One Wish Willow" to win his crush's heart, a hopeless romantic finds himself getting exactly what he asked for but soon discovers that some desires come at a dark, sinister price.

verdict.reason: Watch it tonight for a horror-romance that balances genuine scares with emotional stakes. Barker executes the premise with visual ingenuity, turning the wish-granting conceit into something visually unsettling rather than cute.

ratings.plot: When a menace known as the Joker wreaks havoc and chaos on the people of Gotham, Batman, James Gordon and Harvey Dent must work together to put an end to the madness.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Metrograph is showing the 35mm print, which is the only way to see Nolan's compositions as intended.

ratings.plot: After a threat from the tiger Shere Khan forces him to flee the jungle, a man-cub named Mowgli embarks on a journey of self discovery with the help of panther Bagheera and free-spirited bear Baloo.

verdict.reason: Favreau's photorealistic animation remains a technical marvel that demands the theatrical image. Metrograph's 35mm print is the ideal way to see the jungle rendered at this scale and clarity.

ratings.plot: When her grandson is kidnapped during the Tour de France, Madame Souza and her beloved pooch Bruno team up with the Belleville Sisters--an aged song-and-dance team from the days of Fred Astaire--to rescue him.

verdict.reason: A masterwork of visual storytelling that earns every minute of its runtime through meticulous hand-drawn animation and pure cinematic invention. Chomet builds entire sequences around silence and sight gags rather than dialogue, a discipline that demands the focused attention only a theater provides.

movies.title: There Once Was a Singing Blackbird

ratings.plot: A carefree young percussionist roams the streets of Tbilisi, interacting with friends and strangers alike, and tries to avoid responsibilities.

verdict.reason: A rare Iosseliani film at Metrograph—see it while it's there. The director's deadpan humor and fluid street cinema feel essential on the big screen after 54 years.

ratings.plot: Mysterious boat returns to a village 30 years after vanishing. Two men join its crew hoping for better fortune. After one voyage, they find themselves transported back in time, mistaken for the original crew.

verdict.reason: Mark Jenkin makes films that reward patient, attentive viewing on the big screen, and this one blends temporal mystery with the kind of formal precision his work demands. The 114-minute runtime is a commitment, but Jenkin's control of image and sound justifies the ask in a theater.

ratings.plot: Based on Honobu Yonezawa's novel. Set in 16th century Japan, follows Lord Murashige Araki who, besieged in his castle, confronts mysterious crimes and allies with imprisoned strategist Kanbei Kuroda to uncover the truth.

verdict.reason: Kurosawa at his best—a period mystery that uses castle intrigue and moral interrogation to excavate character rather than plot mechanics. The pairing of a besieged lord with a caged strategist builds tension through dialogue and deception, not spectacle.

ratings.plot: As her mother Sandy (Gretchen Mol) grapples with an uncertain diagnosis, autistic 22-year-old Margarita (a revelatory Lillian Carrier) must reluctantly grow up.

verdict.reason: A debut feature that finds real comedy and tenderness in the specificity of autistic life without turning it into inspiration porn. Lillian Carrier's performance is the kind of breakthrough that justifies the theatrical trip.

ratings.plot: Carrie White, a shy, friendless teenage girl who is sheltered by her domineering, religious mother, unleashes her telekinetic powers after being humiliated by her classmates at her senior prom.

verdict.reason: De Palma's horror masterpiece belongs on the big screen, where the split-screen prom sequence and Sissy Spacek's performance hit hardest. The Alamo locations will pack it with the right crowd.

ratings.plot: In a strange and isolated chateau, a man becomes acquainted with a woman and insists that they have met before.

verdict.reason: One of cinema's great puzzles about memory and desire—Resnais constructs a labyrinth of image and sound that demands the big screen to fully disorient you. The film's geometric compositions and hypnotic editing create a spatial experience that collapses on a TV.

ratings.plot: A former San Francisco police detective juggles wrestling with his personal demons and becoming obsessed with the hauntingly beautiful woman he has been hired to trail, who may be deeply disturbed.

verdict.reason: One of the great films about obsession and desire—see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where Hitchcock's compositional mastery and color palette demand a big screen. The restoration brings out details in every frame that justify the trip.

ratings.plot: Alice, an ambitious camgirl, wakes up one day to discover she's been replaced on her show with an exact replica of herself.

verdict.reason: A smart horror film about identity and digital labor that uses its premise to say something true about performance and violation. Goldhaber sustains the tension through tight 94 minutes and finds real dread in the uncanny—the double isn't a jump-scare trick but a slowly darkening mirror.

ratings.plot: A photographer and her girlfriend are roommates. She is stuck with small-change shooting jobs and dreams of success. When her roommate decides to get married and leave, she feels hurt and has to learn how to deal with living alone.

verdict.reason: A rare chance to see Claudia Weill's 1978 debut on a big screen, a film that defined independent cinema before the term became marketing. The naturalistic acting and New York City photography will look sharper in a theater than anywhere else.

ratings.plot: In 2075, a girl witnesses a mysterious boy in a rainbow suit fall from the sky. He comes from an idyllic far future where time travel is possible. She shelters him and will do whatever it takes to help him return to his time.

verdict.reason: A visually inventive animated film about time and connection that justifies the theatrical screen. The rainbow suit and sky-fall imagery signal a director working in pure visual storytelling rather than exposition.

ratings.plot: Two 12-year-olds, who live on an island, fall in love with each other and elope into the wilderness. While people set out on a search mission, a violent storm approaching them catches their attention.

verdict.reason: Anderson's most purely joyful film deserves the big screen, and 94 minutes means no endurance test. The composition, color, and symmetry reward theatrical projection in ways streaming cannot touch.

ratings.plot: When greedy tycoons refuse to return Mothra's egg to the people of Infant Island, they must decide if they are willing to answer Japan's own pleas for help when Godzilla arises near Nagoya.

verdict.reason: This is peak Toho kaiju craft from Honda at his most confident, balancing spectacle with genuine visual wit. The miniature work and suit choreography in the final battle remain thrilling on a big screen, and the film's satirical edge about corporate greed bites harder than most monster movies ever dare.

ratings.plot: Two bounty killers with similar intentions but different motivations team up to take down a psychotic Mexican outlaw before he and his gang can carry out an audacious bank robbery.

verdict.reason: This is essential Leone—the middle film where his style fully crystallizes and the spaghetti western becomes high art. Clint Eastwood and Lee Van Cleef's face-off plays differently on a big screen, and the musical cues Morricone built around their duel reward theatrical attention.

ratings.plot: Two neighbors form a strong bond after both suspect extramarital activities of their spouses. However, they agree to keep their bond platonic so as not to commit similar wrongs.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai's masterwork demands the big screen—the jewel-toned cinematography and obsessive framing of desire lose their spell on anything smaller. The film moves at its own tempo, and theatrical immersion is the only way to let it work.

ratings.plot: Two teenage boys must escape a violent entity that takes the form of the person they desire most - each other.

verdict.reason: A rare horror film that uses desire and body horror as genuine emotional stakes rather than cheap scares. The 88-minute runtime and Adrian Chiarella's control of tone make this theatrical-only viewing necessary to catch the full impact of its final act.

This is essential anime cinema—a brutal, visionary final statement that dismantles its own narrative and reaches for something genuinely transgressive. The theatrical experience matters here; the assault of sound design and image on a big screen is part of what makes it unforgettable.

ratings.plot: A filmmaking family finds themselves in a real-life horror movie when a body turns up on the set of their low-budget slasher, forcing them to cover up the murder to keep filming.

verdict.reason: Skip the streaming wait and catch this high-concept comedy-horror on the big screen where the tonal shifts land hardest. The 81-minute runtime means no fat, and that premise needs the sudden violence of theatrical sound to work.

ratings.plot: Woody, Buzz, Jessie and the rest of the gang's jobs are challenged when they're introduced to electronics, a new threat to playtime.

verdict.reason: Pixar's core franchise still delivers genuine emotion and invention where it counts. Stanton's involvement suggests the film won't settle for nostalgia alone.

ratings.plot: After a botched bank robbery lands his younger brother in prison, Connie Nikas embarks on a twisted odyssey through New York City's underworld to get his brother Nick out of jail.

verdict.reason: Watch it. The Safdies pack 102 minutes with kinetic tension and Adam Sandler doing raw, desperate work, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the nocturnal neon palette that makes this film move.

movies.title: We're All Going to the World's Fair

ratings.plot: Alone in her attic bedroom, teenager Casey becomes immersed in an online role-playing horror game, wherein she begins to document the changes that may or may not be happening to her.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun's debut captures the disorienting blur between online ritual and genuine psychological unraveling with unnerving precision. The found-footage aesthetic and real-time screen recordings make the dread feel immediate and tactile in ways streaming cannot replicate.

ratings.plot: Two boys meet at an opera training school in Peking in 1924. Their resulting friendship will span nearly 70 years and endure some of the most troublesome times in China's history.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films about art, desire, and political upheaval in 20th-century China—see it on a big screen where the Peking opera performances and cinematography can breathe. Chen Kaige's control of scale and intimacy across 171 minutes justifies every second, especially the way he frames the friendship against the wreckage of history.

movies.title: What Do We See When We Look at the Sky?

ratings.plot: A chance encounter on a street corner has Lisa and Giorgi fall in love at first sight, but an evil spell is cast on them. Will they ever meet again?

verdict.reason: A rare, visionary film that demands the big screen and rewards your full attention for two and a half hours. Koberidze shoots Tbilisi like a living character, and the spell-curse structure is so inventive it makes conventional romance look tired.

ratings.plot: Intent on seeing the Cahulawassee River before it's dammed and turned into a lake, outdoor fanatic Lewis Medlock takes his friends on a canoeing trip they'll never forget into the dangerous American back-country.

verdict.reason: One of the great survival films—see it on 35mm at Metrograph, where Boorman's control of landscape and danger plays at full force. The river itself becomes the antagonist, and the print restores details in light and shadow that streaming flattens.

movies.title: The Night is Short Walk on Girl

ratings.plot: In this comedy about one epic night in Kyoto, a college sophomore goes on a series of surreal encounters with the local nightlife, all the while unaware of the romantic longings of her classmate Senpai.

verdict.reason: Masaaki Yuasa's fluid, inventive animation transforms a single night into a cascade of visual gags and surreal set pieces that demand a theater screen. The 92-minute runtime clips along with enough formal energy to justify the trip.

ratings.plot: In the mid-19th century a mute woman is sent to New Zealand along with her young daughter and prized piano for an arranged marriage to a farmer, but is soon lusted after by a farm worker.

verdict.reason: One of the essential films of the 1990s—see it on a big screen where Campion's visual obsession with light, cloth, and flesh hits hardest. The piano itself becomes a character through sound design that no home system can replicate.

ratings.plot: Two melancholic Hong Kong policemen fall in love: one with a mysterious female underworld figure, the other with a beautiful and ethereal waitress at a late-night restaurant he frequents.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-wai's neon-soaked Hong Kong romance belongs on the biggest screen possible. The handheld camera work and Faye Wong's convenience store dance sequence lose magic at home.

ratings.plot: Arriving in Chicago, Henry moves in with ex-con acquaintance Otis and starts schooling him in the ways of the serial killer.

verdict.reason: This is essential viewing on a big screen—a landmark film about violence that refuses to aestheticize or exploit what it shows. McNaughton's deadpan direction and grainy 16mm stock make the brutality feel documentary-real in a way that home viewing completely loses.

ratings.plot: A young Shaolin follower reunites with his discouraged brothers to form a soccer team using their martial art skills to their advantage.

verdict.reason: Stephen Chow's kinetic blend of wire-fu and sports comedy deserves the big screen treatment. The digital effects that looked cheap in 2001 now play as deliberately cartoonish in the best possible way.

ratings.plot: Elliot lands a job for Erika Tracy as her sexual muse.

verdict.reason: Gregg Araki returning to feature filmmaking after years away deserves a theater audience. The 90-minute runtime and comedy-drama blend suggest a nimble, lived-in piece rather than a studio exercise.

ratings.plot: A fading celebrity takes a black-market drug: a cell-replicating substance that helps her create a younger, better version of herself.

verdict.reason: Coralie Fargeat builds a genuinely disorienting body-horror vision out of vanity and decay that demands a theatrical audience to land properly. The 141-minute runtime and grotesque practical effects need the dark and sound design of a cinema to work.

ratings.plot: A senior chef lives with his three grown daughters; the middle one finds her future plans affected by unexpected events and the life changes of the other household members.

verdict.reason: Ang Lee's debut is a warm, precisely observed film about desire and family obligation that rewards close attention on a big screen. The cooking sequences and intimate domestic scenes have a tactile grace that loses real impact at home.

ratings.plot: A music group of girls need to learn to play a song before the school festival.

verdict.reason: Yamashita captures the genuine chaos of four teenagers learning to play rock in two weeks with a light touch that never condescends to the characters or the form. The film lives in the small moments of frustration and breakthrough, and the final performance earns every second of setup.

ratings.plot: Members of a street gang known as the Warriors must fight their way from the Bronx to their home turf on Coney Island when they are falsely accused of assassinating a respected gang leader.

verdict.reason: Essential theatrical experience for Hill's masterclass in kinetic editing and urban mythology. The film transforms New York's subway tunnels into a neon-lit gauntlet that demands the big screen treatment.

ratings.plot: A professor in revolutionary Iran secretly gathers her most dedicated students to read forbidden classics of Western literature.

verdict.reason: Eran Riklis directs a story about intellectual resistance with real stakes and moral weight. The 107-minute runtime moves fast enough to sustain the tension of forbidden reading in a hostile state.

ratings.plot: When an unconfident young woman is cursed with an old body by a spiteful witch, her only chance of breaking the spell lies with a self-indulgent yet insecure young wizard and his companions in his legged, walking castle.

verdict.reason: This is essential Miyazaki—a fully realized fantasy with animation that rewards the big screen and a romance that actually earns its weight. The character design and the way the castle itself moves and transforms justify the theatrical experience.

ratings.plot: Showgirls Lorelei Lee and Dorothy Shaw travel to Paris, pursued by a private detective hired by the suspicious father of Lorelei's fiancé, as well as a rich, enamored old man and many other doting admirers.

verdict.reason: One of Hawks' sharpest comedies and an essential Marilyn Monroe performance on the big screen. The chemistry between Monroe and Jane Russell, the musical numbers, and the precise comic timing reward theatrical viewing in a way no smaller screen can match.

ratings.plot: Legendary New York poet Ed Saxberger's forgotten works captivate an eccentric group of young creatives, reigniting his artistic passion. Their intrigue intertwines with the bewitching presence of actress Gloria.

verdict.reason: Kent Jones brings his gift for intimate character study to a film about artistic resurrection that earns its emotional stakes without sentimentality. The 90-minute runtime moves with the precision of poetry itself, and watching a forgotten artist find new life through unexpected connection is the kind of small, true thing cinema does best.

ratings.plot: A movie sound recordist accidentally records the evidence that proves that a car accident was actually murder and consequently finds himself in danger.

verdict.reason: De Palma's best thriller, a masterwork of paranoid cinema that demands the big screen for its elaborate setpieces and sound design. The climax alone—a meticulously constructed sequence at the Liberty Day parade—justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: A woman starts exhibiting increasingly disturbing behavior after asking her husband for a divorce. Suspicions of infidelity soon give way to something much more sinister.

verdict.reason: Zulawski's 1981 vision of marital collapse and cosmic horror is a rare theatrical event that demands the big screen's immersion. The practical creature effects and Isabelle Adjani's unhinged performance need cinema's scale to hit with full force.

ratings.plot: A cab driver finds himself the hostage of an engaging contract killer as he makes his rounds from hit to hit during one night in Los Angeles.

verdict.reason: Mann's night-vision Los Angeles is a character unto itself, and the cat-and-mouse dialogue between Cruise and Foxx justifies the theatrical investment. Tom Cruise's silver-haired killer is one of cinema's most magnetic villains, and Mann shoots the city with the precision of a heist film.

ratings.plot: Amidst turmoil and racial conflict in a Francophone African state, a white French woman fights for her coffee crop, her family and ultimately for her life.

verdict.reason: Denis makes a furious, uncompromising film about complicity and refusal to leave—watch it for the clarity of her moral vision. The final thirty minutes contain some of her most brutal and precise filmmaking.

ratings.plot: Green Beret veteran Rambo takes on a Pacific Northwest sheriff and the National Guard.

verdict.reason: This is a lean, tense thriller that works better than the sequels that buried its actual point about trauma and institutional cruelty. Sylvester Stallone's performance is genuinely affecting, and Ted Kotcheff keeps the action grounded in real geography and consequence for 93 minutes that don't waste a frame.

ratings.plot: A boy is left to his own devices when his mother refuses to pay for his schooling.

verdict.reason: Eustache's rare 1974 film about childhood neglect cuts deeper than sentiment—it observes how indifference shapes a kid's resourcefulness. Metrograph is the only place to see it, and this restoration belongs on the big screen.

ratings.plot: Two city-bred siblings are stranded in the Australian Outback, where they learn to survive with the aid of an Aboriginal boy on his "walkabout": a ritual separation from his tribe.

verdict.reason: Roeg's visual command of the Outback is unmatched on small screens, and this 35mm print at Metrograph restores the color and light that define the film's language. The cinematography is the story.

ratings.plot: A couple take a trip to Argentina but both men find their lives drifting apart in opposite directions.

verdict.reason: Wong Kar-Wai at his peak, using Buenos Aires and a 16mm camera to turn a breakup into pure visual poetry. The cinematography alone justifies the theatrical trip—those neon-soaked interiors and rain-streaked streets demand a big screen.

ratings.plot: A young martial artist is caught between respecting his pacifist father's wishes or stopping a group of disrespectful foreigners from stealing precious artifacts.

verdict.reason: Jackie Chan at peak physical comedy—this is essential 90s action cinema that rewards the big screen. The drunken style choreography is intricate enough to demand theatrical clarity, and Chan's willingness to wreck his body for a gag plays best when you can see every impact.

ratings.plot: New Orleans District Attorney Jim Garrison discovers there's more to the Kennedy assassination than the official story.

verdict.reason: Stone's three-hour investigation into the Kennedy assassination remains essential American cinema, and the layered editing, cross-cutting between film stocks, and performance ensemble justify the theatrical commitment. The visual complexity of the courtroom sequences and Stone's formal ambition demand a big screen.

ratings.plot: A teenager just trying to make it through life in the suburbs is introduced by a classmate to a mysterious late-night TV show.

verdict.reason: Schoenbrun builds genuine dread from the collision between suburban dissociation and a show that bleeds into reality in ways that feel earned and strange. The 100-minute runtime keeps the uncanny tension taut without overstaying its welcome.

ratings.plot: After Queen Elizabeth I commands him not to grow old, a young nobleman struggles with love and his place in the world.

verdict.reason: Sally Potter's audacious formal experiment transforms Virginia Woolf into pure cinema, collapsing centuries into a single luminous body. The visual wit of the costume and gender shifts, especially in the abrupt transitions between eras, justifies the theatrical experience over any smaller screen.

ratings.plot: A day in the life of an unfaithful married couple and their steadily deteriorating relationship.

verdict.reason: Antonioni's masterwork on marital dissolution demands the theater—a film about emotional distance that only works at full scale. Metrograph's print restores the compositions and silences that make this 1961 film feel like cinema itself being reinvented.

ratings.plot: The ethereally beautiful Vicky recalls her romances with Hao Hao and Jack in the neon-lit clubs of Taipei.

verdict.reason: Hou Hsiao-hsien's nocturnal Taipei is hypnotic and formally precise, worth experiencing on a theater screen where the neon saturates the darkness. The 119-minute runtime demands patience, but the payoff is a film that moves like memory—fractured, sensual, and resistant to easy explanation.

ratings.plot: Two roommates/physical therapists, one a vain woman and the other an awkward teenager, share an increasingly bizarre relationship.

verdict.reason: Altman's most enigmatic film demands the big screen and patient attention to its dreamlike logic. Metrograph is the right venue for a 1977 masterpiece that rewards repeated viewings and rewards argument.

ratings.plot: A school student who conspires with his teacher and others to overthrow the Qing Dynasty sees his family slaughtered at the hands of his enemies. He joins the Shaolin Temple and rigorously studies martial arts to avenge his belove...

verdict.reason: Essential martial arts cinema that invented the training-montage template and still moves with purpose and clarity. Metrograph is showing a restored 35mm print of Liu Chia-liang's masterpiece of choreography and narrative structure.

ratings.plot: A reclusive retired professor is faced with confronting modernity when a group of vulgar youths led by an obnoxious marchesa take up residence in his unused upper residence.

verdict.reason: Visconti's final film is a masterwork of class collision and moral decay, essential viewing at Metrograph where its restoration reveals the precision of every frame. Burt Lancaster's performance as the professor contains multitudes in near-silence, doing more with restraint than most actors manage with dialogue.

ratings.plot: After a car wreck on Mulholland Drive renders a woman amnesiac, she and a Hollywood-hopeful search for clues and answers across Los Angeles in a twisting venture beyond dreams and reality.

verdict.reason: One of Lynch's essential films and a masterwork of narrative architecture that demands the big screen. The 147-minute runtime and layered sound design reward full theatrical immersion.

ratings.plot: A disfigured composer sells his soul for the woman he loves so that she will perform his music, but an evil record tycoon betrays him and steals his music to open his rock palace, The Paradise.

verdict.reason: De Palma's 1974 fusion of Faust, The Phantom of the Opera, and rock opera is a formally dazzling cult film that rewards the big screen. The split-screen sequences, tracking shots, and operatic excess are built for theatrical immersion, not home viewing.

ratings.plot: During Prohibition, Treasury agent Eliot Ness sets out to stop ruthless Chicago gangster Al Capone, and assembles a small, incorruptible team to help him.

verdict.reason: De Palma's command of suspense and his ensemble cast—anchored by Connery's scene-stealing turn—make this a theatrical experience that hasn't dated. The ballroom shootout and Union Station massacre sequences demand a big screen and a crowd.

ratings.plot: In 1955 New Orleans, small-time private investigator Harry Angel is hired by a man who calls himself Louis Cypher to track down a singer named Johnny Favorite, but the investigation takes an unexpected and somber turn.

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm print of Parker's 1955 New Orleans descent into the demonic, where every shadow and reflection matters. The restoration and format make this noir-horror hybrid a full sensory experience.

ratings.plot: A young student is devastated when he finds that his girlfriend is cheating on him. In order to find out why she did it, he decides to spy on her and her lover.

verdict.reason: Rohmer's moral precision about jealousy and self-deception cuts deeper than any thriller about infidelity. Metrograph's print restores the deliberate pacing that makes watching someone rationalize their worst impulses feel like real life.

ratings.plot: A disgraced ex-policeman who runs a small ring of prostitutes finds himself in a race against time when one of his women goes missing.

verdict.reason: Na Hong-jin's debut is a masterclass in tension and moral ambiguity that demands the big screen. Metrograph is showing it on 35mm, the only way to catch the film's savage energy and grimy Seoul cinematography in theaters.

ratings.plot: During the Vietnam War, a soldier finds himself the outsider of his own squad when they unnecessarily kidnap a female villager, for their sexual enjoyment.

verdict.reason: De Palma's unflinching anatomy of moral collapse in a combat unit deserves the big screen. The cinematography uses color and composition to isolate the protagonist within his own squad, making his isolation physical and unbearable.

ratings.plot: On a dark, wet night a historic and regal Chinese cinema sees its final film. Together with a small handful of souls they bid "Goodbye, Dragon Inn".

verdict.reason: Tsai's elegy for cinema is itself a cinematic act, shot almost entirely in static long shots, silence, and the ambient presence of a dying movie palace. It's a film that can only work in a theater, and it works as a near-perfect argument for why theaters matter.

ratings.plot: A prince enlists a thief to serve as his bodyguard to protect him from assassins.

verdict.reason: Chia-Liang Liu's 1979 action-comedy is a rare theatrical revival of a Shaw Brothers standout that rewards the trip. The fight choreography and tonal balance between slapstick and genuine peril remain sharp on the big screen at Metrograph.

ratings.plot: Macbeth, the Thane of Glamis, receives a prophecy from a trio of witches that one day he will become King of Scotland. Consumed by ambition and spurred to action by his wife, Macbeth murders his king and takes the throne for himself.

verdict.reason: Kurzel strips the play down to blood and ambition, shooting it like a brutal medieval siege rather than a costume drama. The heavy use of smoke, shadow, and handheld camera work makes the violence feel immediate and the supernatural elements genuinely unsettling on a big screen.

Wong Kar-wai's restored cut transforms a notoriously difficult film into something radiant and newly legible. The 4K restoration reveals color and texture that were lost in the original, making the visual poetry worth experiencing on a theater screen.

ratings.plot: A middle-aged playboy becomes fascinated by the daughter of a private detective who has been hired to entrap him with the wife of a client.

verdict.reason: Wilder's best work on desire and deception deserves the big screen, and this 130-minute film moves with the precision of a Swiss watch despite its length. The chemistry between Cary Grant and Audrey Hepburn carries the moral ambiguity that makes the setup land as comedy rather than creepiness.

ratings.plot: A rough, short-tempered patriarch of a working-class family sees his life and the relationships around him slowly unravel.

verdict.reason: Gary Oldman's only directorial feature is a brutal, uncompromising look at working-class London that demands to be seen in a theater. Metrograph's screening gives access to a film rarely in circulation, one where the dialogue and violence hit harder on the big screen than anywhere else.

ratings.plot: Fausta is suffering from a rare disease called the Milk of Sorrow, which is transmitted through the breast milk of pregnant women who were abused or raped during or soon after pregnancy. While living in constant fear and confusion...

verdict.reason: Claudia Llosa's singular vision—a filmmaker working at the height of her formal powers—demands a big screen and an audience willing to follow her into the strange and visionary. Metrograph is the only place in the city showing it, and a 94-minute film this densely imagined will lose its grip on a smaller format.

ratings.plot: The final sixty-seven days of Van Gogh's life are examined.

verdict.reason: Pialat captures Van Gogh's last weeks with the specificity of lived time rather than biographical machinery. Jacques Dutronc's performance anchors the film in exhaustion and creative fury, not mythmaking.

ratings.plot: A teenage skateboarder's life begins to fray after he is involved in the accidental death of a security guard.

verdict.reason: Watch it. Gus Van Sant's fractured narrative and handheld aesthetic capture adolescent guilt with a formal precision that demands the theater, and Metrograph's 35mm print restores the grain and texture essential to the film's mood.

ratings.plot: Abandoned by his American lover, a handsome teenager from the mountains journeys to Manila in an effort to support his family. With a popular call boy as his mentor, Paul enters the glittering world of male strippers, prostitution...

verdict.reason: Lino Brocka's 1988 film remains a vital document of Manila's sex trade and class collapse, told with unflinching clarity and formal precision. The 136-minute runtime and grainy 35mm print reward patient viewing in a theater where the social texture and visual grain cannot be flattened.

ratings.plot: Reminiscing about his dead son, a Vietnam War veteran attempts to uncover his past while suffering from a severe case of dissociation. To do so, he must decipher reality and life from his own dreams, delusions, and perceptions of ...

verdict.reason: Adrian Lyne builds genuine dread from ambiguity instead of jump scares, letting the camera linger on body horror and wrongness until you stop trusting what you're seeing. The 113 minutes feel earned because every hallucination is shot with the precision of something real.

ratings.plot: Aunt Mei's famous homemade dumplings provide amazing age-defying qualities popular with middle-aged women. But her latest customer - a fading actress - is determined to find out what the secret ingredient is.

verdict.reason: Fruit Chan's body horror is genuinely unsettling and his social satire about vanity cuts deeper than the premise suggests. The final act reveals justify the setup's grotesqueness in a way that lingers long after the runtime ends.

movies.title: IT'S A MAD, MAD, MAD, MAD WORLD

ratings.plot: Several different motorists witness a single car crash in the California desert and, after the driver's dying words indicate the location of a hidden stash of loot, turn against each other in a mad dash across the state to get to it.

verdict.reason: Skip the home version and catch this sprawling slapstick epic on a big screen where the sight gags and ensemble chaos actually land. The 70mm restoration makes the widescreen composition—packed with simultaneous action across the frame—the whole point of the experience.

ratings.plot: A nurse enlists the help of a petty criminal to foil a sinister plot to murder two children.

verdict.reason: Wellman's brisk 72-minute thriller moves like a silent picture even with dialogue, and the pairing of a nurse and a criminal against a murder scheme has genuine suspense. The print restoration matters here—this is a film that breathes on the big screen, not on your laptop.

ratings.plot: A love triangle develops between a vampire, her cellist companion, and a gerontologist.

verdict.reason: Tony Scott's debut is a sensual, formally daring vampire film that rewards the big screen more than it did on release. Metrograph is showing a 35mm print, and the neon-soaked compositions and Bauhaus production design demand to be seen in that format.

ratings.plot: Set on the last day of camp, in the hot summer of 1981, a group of counselors try to complete their unfinished business before the day ends.

verdict.reason: This comedy has become a cult classic that rewards repeat viewing and plays brilliantly in a theater full of people who get the joke. David Wain's absurdist energy and the ensemble's commitment to deadpan nonsense make this a rare case where initial critical dismissal undersells what actually lands on screen.

movies.title: Collier Schorr presents Je tu il elle

verdict.reason: Chantal Akerman's 1974 autofiction landmark demands the big screen and Schorr's curation adds interpretive weight. The film's real power lives in its unbroken takes and the specific grain of 16mm—a home viewing flattens what makes it singular.

Chantal Akerman's debut is a landmark of feminist cinema and sexual candor that demands the big screen. The 65mm restoration and unbroken takes reveal the formal rigor that makes this film's intimacy so unsettling.

movies.title: The Bakery Girl of Monceau + Suzanne's Career

verdict.reason: Skip this if you need plot or spectacle, but watch it if you want to see Rohmer invent the language of modern cinema from a café table. These twin films are the foundation of everything that followed—shot on 16mm with the texture of memory, dialogue that feels like eavesdropping, and a camera that trusts you to find the meaning in a glance.

ratings.plot: Mongols with the help of an insider, ambush the influential Yang Family, defenders of the dynasty. The Mongols must hunt down all Yang survivors so their insidious plot to overthrow the dynasty will not be uncovered.

verdict.reason: Chia-Liang Liu builds his action around a single weapon and a single family fighting system with a precision that rewards close viewing on the biggest screen possible. The pole choreography is both geometric and brutal, shot with clarity that modern action films have mostly abandoned.

A newly struck print of Tsai Ming-liang's masterpiece deserves the big screen, and this is likely your only chance to see it projected as intended. The image restoration restores the film's glacial compositions and deadpan color palette to their full, agonizing power.

ratings.plot: N/A

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm screening of a vital documentary about women's labor and dignity that deserves theater sound and image. Metrograph's print is the reason to go tonight instead of waiting for a smaller screen.

ratings.plot: In early twentieth century China, various criminals with different goals are connected to a Shanghai train, with many rich people on-board.

verdict.reason: Sammo Hung orchestrates a locomotive heist with the kinetic precision and humor that makes 1980s Hong Kong action cinema essential viewing. The train setting gives every stunt and fight sequence a built-in spatial logic that elevates the chaos above standard ensemble action.

movies.title: Solaris preceded by The Working End

verdict.reason: Tarkovsky's three-hour masterpiece demands the big screen and the complete theatrical experience, especially paired with a short that deepens its themes. The restoration brings out the luminous cinematography that defines the film's power to isolate and haunt.

ratings.plot: Tally Brown was a classically trained opera and blues singer, and a star of underground films in New York City. Brown opens the film with a cover of David Bowie's "Heroes" and concludes with "Rock 'n' Roll Suicide."

verdict.reason: A rare 1979 document of an underground New York fixture performing her own music on film—see it for von Praunheim's direct, unfiltered approach to capturing a singular artist. The Bowie bookends and blues-opera range show a performer working without commercial constraint or apology.

movies.title: SWISS MISS with Them Thar Hills

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're committed to sitting through two Laurel and Hardy shorts back-to-back on the big screen. The pairing offers no particular restoration, rarity, or theatrical argument that justifies the trip over streaming.

movies.title: RASQUACHISMO: THE EARLY WORK OF LUIS VALDEZ

verdict.reason: Essential documentation of a radical Chicano theater pioneer whose work shaped American political performance. The film captures Valdez's formal innovation and urgency during the farmworker movement when theater was not a safe space but a weapon.

movies.title: SONS OF THE DESERT with Busy Bodies

verdict.reason: Two-reel Laurel and Hardy shorts belong on the big screen where their physical timing and facial expressions land hardest. The pairing gives you nearly 45 minutes of pure slapstick craft from the silent era's sharpest comedy duo.

This is a rare chance to see a Broadway phenomenon on film, and it captures the theatrical magic that made the show essential live. The orchestrations and Rachel Zegler's voice carry an intimacy that only a camera can provide.

ratings.plot: Verdi's famous opera is brought to life in this production. The immortal tale of the noble Moor and his beautiful young wife, and of his lieutenant, whose jealousy and lust for power lead him to commit the ultimate treason.

verdict.reason: Zeffirelli's 1986 operatic adaptation demands the theater's sound system and scale—this is not a film to compress at home. Plácido Domingo's Otello and the lush orchestration of Verdi justify the subway ride and ticket price.

ratings.plot: Exploding out of the AGFA vaults as a brand-new 35mm preservation, this 1990s kung fu fantasia from Hong Kong is a breathtaking combination of action, comedy, and cooking.

verdict.reason: A rare 35mm restoration of a Hong Kong kung fu film from the vaults demands the big screen. The 89-minute runtime and blend of action, comedy, and cooking make this a singular theatrical experience that justifies the trip.

ratings.plot: Oscilloscope Laboratories presents CATVIDEOFEST 2026, a compilation of the latest and best cat videos culled from countless hours of unique submissions and sourced animations, music videos, and classic internet powerhouses. Each year, across the country, local theaters partner with nearby cat-focused charities, animal welfare associations, and shelters alike – a portion of ticket proceeds from every show goes directly to local cats in need.

verdict.reason: Seventy-five minutes of uncut cat content on a theater screen is the rare occasion when collective laughter beats solitary scrolling. Ticket proceeds go to local shelters, so you're funding rescue work while getting exactly what you came for.

ratings.plot: One voice. One unforgettable spectacle. SIA: NOSTALGIC FOR THE PRESENT is a bold, genre-defying experience that trades pop pageantry for pure artistry. Awe-inspiring vocals, breathtaking choreography, and iconic performances, captured cinematically and soundtracked by an unmatched catalog of hits. In 2016, Sia toured the world, mirroring this film live on stage, frame for frame. Remastered for its tenth anniversary, it stands alone for the first time – not as a concert film, but as a visual masterpiece unlike anything in music since. Starring Maddie Ziegler, Kristen Wiig, Paul Dano, Ben Mendelsohn, Gaby Hoffmann, and Tig Notaro. Choreographed by Ryan Heffington. Directed by Sia and Daniel Askill.

verdict.reason: A remastered tenth-anniversary release of a singular piece of visual art that was never meant to be a concert film in the first place. The 75-minute runtime and Ryan Heffington's choreography justify the theatrical commitment in a way streaming cannot match.

ratings.plot: Imagine that a local cable station was invaded by otherdimensional creatures at the stroke of midnight. That's Video Vortex. Each month, this series presents a mystery transmission that's culled from the outer limits of home video history – from essential underground films to surreal docs, from tokusatsu battle-parties to outsider experiments. So warm up the cathode tubes, dim the lights, and let your senses intermingle with the glow.

verdict.reason: Skip your streaming queue and catch this month's transmission on a real screen where the analog glow and theatrical darkness matter. Video Vortex specializes in obscure home video finds that demand the communal, unfiltered experience of a theater.

ratings.plot: A musical juxtaposition of the Orpheus/Eurydice and Hades/Persephone myths that examines the way real life can impact our quest for a perfect world.

verdict.reason: This is a Broadway phenomenon that demands the theatrical experience of live performance and orchestral sound. The staging of dual mythologies intertwined—Orpheus chasing Eurydice while Hades and Persephone's relationship crumbles—creates visual and emotional architecture that only works in a theater.

ratings.plot: A traveling psychic who helps lost souls cross over encounters a powerful entity at a remote house. While investigating its origins, she uncovers dark secrets and faces a deadly threat from an unexpected source.

verdict.reason: A competent haunted-house setup squanders its premise on jump scares and predictable twists that feel like filler in a film that doesn't earn its runtime. The psychic-investigator angle collapses into standard possession tropes, and there's no visual or narrative reason to see this in a theater rather than at home.

ratings.plot: A slow, quiet Christmas Eve night at the police station turns into strange horror after a man enters claiming he wants to confess to murder.

verdict.reason: The premise collapses under its own weight, and the execution does not justify the runtime. A 96-minute film that feels designed for streaming drains the theatrical experience of any payoff.

ratings.plot: Follows the Jackass crew as they perform their final series of dangerous stunts and pranks, marking the end of the franchise.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a clip reel masquerading as a finale, not worth a theater ticket when you own the originals. The 92-minute runtime is padding around footage you've already seen, and the theatrical experience adds nothing that a home rewatch wouldn't deliver.

ratings.plot: A man raised by Santa's elves travels from the North Pole to New York City to meet his biological father, who doesn't know he exists and is in desperate need of some Christmas spirit.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a streaming-era comfort watch that loses nothing on a smaller screen and plays better at home on repeat. The Alamo screenings offer no format advantage, restoration, or theatrical rarity that justifies the trip over your couch.

movies.title: Gail Daughtry and the Celebrity Sex Pass

ratings.plot: When her fiancé uses their "celebrity pass" agreement, Midwest bride Gail Daughtry travels to Hollywood seeking revenge by pursuing her own celebrity encounter.

verdict.reason: A thin premise stretched thin by a runtime that still feels long. David Wain's direction can't elevate sitcom-level material about relationship revenge fantasies.

ratings.plot: In 1970s Detroit, John Miller falls for a local gangster's girl. In retaliation, the gangster enacts a frame job to send the innocent man to prison. Life ruined, Miller plots a revenge campaign against the man who took his girl away.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the revenge setup is familiar enough that uneven execution and a 103-minute runtime that doesn't justify itself make this a better streaming choice. Potsy Ponciroli's direction doesn't do enough with 1970s Detroit to earn a theatrical trip.

ratings.plot: Unpopular schoolgirl Jenna Rink makes an unusual wish on her birthday. Miraculously, her wish comes true and the 13-year-old Jenna wakes up the next day as a 30-year-old woman.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this mid-tier rom-com fantasy is better suited to a lazy afternoon at home than a theater trip. The premise has worn thin in two decades, and a standard multiplexing at the Alamo doesn't offer anything that justifies the seat.
Skip it; the premise does not justify a theater ticket and the execution does not compensate. The runtime and pacing will test your patience more than reward it at home.

ratings.plot: A grieving father enacts his long-awaited revenge against a ruthless gang on Christmas Eve.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Woo's action direction can't overcome a thin revenge premise that has been executed better elsewhere. The 104-minute runtime still feels stretched for a story this straightforward.

ratings.plot: What seems to be the ideal setting for fun and relaxation quickly turns deadly when six vacationing college students encounter a cursed spirit with an insatiable appetite.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a forgettable slasher with no distinctive voice or visual style. The creature design and kills lack the ingenuity needed to justify a theatrical trip over streaming at home.

ratings.plot: A young George Washington faces war, betrayal, and impossible choices that will forge a leader.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you have a specific appetite for faith-based historical action. Jon Erwin's direction prioritizes inspirational narrative over cinematic craft, and the 125-minute runtime stretches a thin premise past its breaking point.

ratings.plot: Newcomers to the country-music business seek love and stardom.

verdict.reason: Bogdanovich's touch has abandoned him here, leaving a sitcom-flat romantic drama that mistakes Nashville scenery for character. The 116-minute runtime tests patience for a film that resolves nothing with any conviction.

ratings.plot: Los Angeles police officer Brian O'Conner must decide where his loyalty really lies when he becomes enamored with the street racing world he has been sent undercover to end it.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the theatrical cut is a clunky undercover procedural that hasn't aged well and the sequels have completely eclipsed the original. The Alamo screenings offer no restoration, format upgrade, or special event context that would justify the trip over streaming.

ratings.plot: Four teenagers discover an underground fallout shelter thanks to a friend, who agrees to have them hide there with the door locked for a few days to escape a school trip. Yet, time passes, and their friend doesn't come back to get...

verdict.reason: A tense chamber piece about confinement and teenage psychology that works best as a locked-room thriller, though the execution is uneven and the runtime drags in the second half. Nick Hamm's direction squeezes real dread from the premise, but the payoff doesn't justify sitting through 102 minutes of escalating claustrophobia.

ratings.plot: Two friends find themselves caught up in mayhem involving killers, monsters and supernatural creatures once again.

verdict.reason: Franchise fatigue has set in hard, and the comedic aim is wildly off. This entry feels like it's performing the motions of parody without landing anything sharp.

ratings.plot: A hypnotic, unhinged thriller with an original story promising plenty of glamour, sex, and violence.

verdict.reason: Refn's visual obsessions can justify a theatrical gamble even when the script falters, but this one tests patience with uneven execution. The 109-minute runtime and glossy genre trappings matter less than whether you trust him to sustain mood over narrative coherence.

ratings.plot: Julian, a drug-smuggler thriving in Bangkok's criminal underworld, sees his life get even more complicated when his mother compels him to find and kill whoever is responsible for his brother's recent death.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Refn's visual control cannot salvage a script that mistakes silence for depth and punishment for meaning. The neon palette is arresting, but two hours of a blank protagonist absorbing blows grows tedious fast.

ratings.plot: The early life of musician Michael Jackson, from the discovery of his talent as the lead of the Jackson Five to the artist whose creative ambition fueled a pursuit to become the biggest entertainer in the world.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Fuqua's flatly composed biopic reduces Jackson's complexity to a conventional rise-and-fall template. The 127-minute runtime drags across familiar beats without the visual or narrative invention the subject demands.

ratings.plot: The parallel coming-of-age stories of a father living in Sarajevo during World War II and his son living through the Siege of Sarajevo during the Bosnian War.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the premise of remaking a film about remaking doesn't justify the runtime or conceptual repetition. The execution collapses under its own meta-joke before the midpoint.

ratings.plot: A family struggling with genetic illnesses lives on a country estate. Personal drama develops amongst them in this intimate portrait.

verdict.reason: Skip it; the execution fails to justify its premise, and 97 minutes of family tension on an estate plays better on a smaller screen. Aïnouz has made sharper work, and this one doesn't warrant the subway ride.

ratings.plot: Bumbling Inspector Clouseau must solve the murder of a famous soccer coach and find out who stole the infamous Pink Panther diamond.

verdict.reason: Steve Martin's Clouseau is a one-note impersonation that mistakes accent work for character, and Shawn Levy's direction serves up sitcom timing instead of the elegant timing Blake Edwards mastered. The 93 minutes feel padded with forced physical comedy that neither builds nor lands.

ratings.plot: The Dhamaal boys are back and ready to chase the "Treasure of Life," facing crazy challenges along the way. What starts as a treasure hunt quickly turns into a rollercoaster of hilarious misadventures.

verdict.reason: A 143-minute Bollywood comedy sequel with no theatrical distinction and a track record of audience indifference. The runtime punishes what is clearly a franchise coasting on nostalgia rather than new ideas.

ratings.plot: Kara Zor-El, aka Supergirl, joins forces with an unlikely companion on an interstellar journey of vengeance and justice when an unexpected adversary strikes too close to home.

verdict.reason: Skip it; Craig Gillespie cannot salvage a fundamentally broken DC blockbuster. The film is playing on standard screens in multiplex chains with no theatrical value to justify sitting through what the response to it has already condemned as a misfire.

movies.title: Once Upon a Time in Beirut

verdict.reason: This debut feature is narratively muddled and struggles to justify its two-hour runtime with underdeveloped characters and plotting. The film's nostalgic framing of Beirut's past feels sentimental rather than earned, offering little that justifies a theater trip over waiting for streaming.

verdict.reason: This is a concert film, not a narrative work, and the theatrical value depends entirely on your relationship to the artist. Unless you're already a devoted FC fan willing to pay for a big-screen experience of a live performance, this belongs at home where you can pause and rewind.

verdict.reason: The film's emotional core doesn't justify the runtime, and the supernatural elements feel grafted onto a story that doesn't need them. At 95 minutes, it still drags through familiar territory without the craft to make it stick.

ratings.plot: A young woman must deliver a top-secret motorcycle to the US military after the man assigned to deliver it, her lover, is murdered by enemy agents.

verdict.reason: Skip it; this is a forgettable 1987 action programmer with no theatrical value or cult appeal. Fred Olen Ray's direction is workmanlike and the plot is a thin excuse to string together chase scenes that play better on home video.

ratings.plot: This is a story of five passionate girls fighting hard in the gaming world, hoping to break the social stereotype. Yet this is more difficult than it seems, with all the unknown challenges ahead.

verdict.reason: The premise of women in gaming is real, but this film arrives without the craft or insight to justify a theatrical ticket. The generic setup and vague synopsis suggest a made-for-streaming indie that will feel smaller on a big screen than on your couch.

ratings.plot: The bonds between humans and animals following a stray dog named Gohan as it moves through life with temporary owners over a decade, through good times and bad times, joy and sorrow, hellos and goodbyes.

The emotional weight hinges entirely on whether you connect with the specific owners' stories, which is a personal call best made knowing the film's pacing and tone first.

verdict.reason: A lean 87-minute film about rekindled desire and messy entanglement has real emotional texture, but it's the kind of intimate character study that works just as well on a smaller screen. Cheng-Chui Kuo shoots the Taipei night with a calm observational eye that rewards patience, though the modest scope and interpersonal focus make this less urgent as a theatrical event.

The extended cut offers more material, but without knowing the director's specific additions or the film's original theatrical merit, the runtime expansion alone doesn't justify a trip. Check runtime and what scenes were restored before committing.

ratings.plot: Richard Wagner's last opera has remained controversial since its first performance for its unique, and, for some, unsavory blending of religious and erotic themes and imagery. Based on one of the medieval epic romances of King Art...

verdict.reason: Syberberg's four-hour operatic vision is uncompromising and visually baroque, but demands absolute commitment and tolerance for his deliberately confrontational staging of Wagner's final work. The theatrical experience is singular, though patience and appetite for avant-garde opera aesthetics are prerequisites.

Browning's direction prioritizes the singers over cinematic language, so you're essentially watching a stage performance captured in a theater.

verdict.reason: A obscure 1975 crime film with a genuinely nasty premise deserves a look if you're hunting for forgotten genre work, but the execution is thin and the runtime doesn't justify the one-note revenge setup. The HDR presentation at Alamo Drafthouse Downtown Brooklyn or Staten Island will make the action sharper than it will be at home, so format matters here.

ratings.plot: A young man searches for the body of his sister years after her tragic disappearance.

ratings.plot: Presented in Japanese with English subtitles Crunchyroll Anime Nights is bringing MOB PSYCHO 100 to the big screen! To celebrate MOB PSYCHO 100's 10th anniversary, we'll be showing 5 amazing episodes – chosen by YOU, the fans – that will take you through all of Mob's story. Mob is an 8th grader with powerful psychic abilities who wants to be normal. When not exorcising evil spirits, he attempts to suppress his powers, causing stunted emotions. But when he hits 100 percent, his pent-up feelings unleash a dark power. Can he survive the psychic strain?

verdict.reason: A fan-curated highlight reel works best if you've already invested in the series, but the theatrical format and communal screening energy reward newcomers willing to jump into the middle of Mob's arc. The 122-minute runtime compresses a ten-year story into peaks rather than foundations, which demands either prior knowledge or tolerance for emotional whiplash.

ratings.plot: 40 YEARS OF FUCKIN' UP is SPINAL TAP, but real. It's a film about the infamous, fairly unfamous, and beloved punk rock band NOFX. This is the unbelievable story about how a group of untalented, drug-addicted teenage punks somehow became the most successful independent band in history – and they did it haphazardly, entirely on their own.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you have real affection for the band or want a brisk, chaotic punk documentary that does not pretend to be anything more. The runtime is lean for a band biography, but the self-aware tone trades depth for speed.

ratings.plot: The Platt family bands together to navigate their new surroundings after a cosmic event transports their suburban neighborhood to someplace unknown.

verdict.reason: Mitchell's visual control and world-building ambition merit the big screen, but a 99-minute runtime suggests the premise gets shortchanged—better as a home watch if the theatrical cut feels rushed. The suburban-to-otherwhere pivot lives or dies on execution, and there's no guarantee a director known for slow-burn dread lands the tonal balance this concept demands.

ratings.plot: A bullied girl transfers schools hoping for peace, but her past trauma isolates her-until she discovers a series of secret letters hidden around the school, leading her on a mysterious quest to uncover their sender's true intent.

verdict.reason: A competent animated drama about isolation and connection, but the mystery-box structure relies on emotional payoff that may not justify the runtime on a big screen. Kim Yong-Hwan's direction is serviceable rather than visually urgent, making this better suited to home viewing unless you need a gentler theatrical option tonight.

movies.title: Six: The Musical Live! Early Screening

ratings.plot: Winner of over 35 awards, experience the best of British musical HER-story in a live capture of the must-see musical sensation, SIX the Musical . The original West End cast reunite at London’s Vaudeville Theatre in front of a sold-out audience to strut their stuff and rewrite their Tudor traumas in an unmissable cinematic recording of the show packed full of style, sass, and sensational songs. Watched by audiences of over 3.5 million, SIX the Musical has become a global theatre phenomenon since its 2017 debut at Edinburgh Festival Fringe, where it has redefined the boundaries of musical theatre. The show tells the extraordinary story of the six wives of King Henry VIII, who step out of the shadow of their infamous husband and reclaim their own narratives.

verdict.reason: A filmed stage performance works best if you cannot see the real thing, but this West End capture on a theater screen lacks the liveness that makes musicals breathe in person. The 98-minute runtime respects your night better than a full stage show, yet you are watching actors perform for cameras in a playhouse, not for you in a cinema.

movies.title: Wet Hot American Summer: 25th Anniversary Party

ratings.plot: Remember those kids who were too cool for school? Those kids are now your camp counselors. David Wain and company (including members of MTV's The State , the Upright Citizens Brigade, SNL , and a pre-famed Bradley Cooper) make idiosyncratic, over-the-top. strangely touching comedy. These character creations are unlike anything you've ever seen AND people you can relate to. There's young love, steamy sessions in the shed, talking cans, and everybody's favorite activity...going to town! So relive this unbelievably watchable, funny, original movie. It doesn't give one single f*ck...and that's the best part.

verdict.reason: Skip a special screening unless you have nostalgia for the original or want to catch the ensemble cast in a room together. The theatrical experience doesn't add much that the home version doesn't deliver, and the film plays better when you can pause it.

ratings.plot: A direct continuation of the first three films in the SAW voyage, SAW IV mutates the format to share the origin story of mysterious serial killer Jigsaw, his traps, and Billy, his faithful puppet. This grimy, unforgiving squirm-machine exchanges the Michael Bay-style action of the previous two entries for an overdose of soap opera histrionics. Plus some of the most vomitously beautiful practical gore effects of the Y2K era. SAW IV is another reminder that this franchise was built to be experienced big, loud, and in a theater full of appreciative gorehounds. To quote Jigsaw: “It’s not over, the games have just begun.”

verdict.reason: The 35mm print at Alamo Drafthouse makes this the rare chance to see franchise gore design at theatrical scale, but the soap opera plotting and bloat test patience even for genre devotees. Practical effects and print quality matter here; streaming kills both.

ratings.plot: A 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain travels to Provincetown and stumbles into the chaotic world of a restaurant kitchen, setting off a summer that will shape the course of his life.

verdict.reason: Matt Johnson's visual precision and control make this prequel origin story worth watching if you trust his direction, but a 106-minute film about a young Bourdain's first kitchen season feels minor next to the man's later life and voice. The Provincetown setting and summer-job framing have charm, but Johnson is working in biographical territory that lacks the urgency of his best work.

ratings.plot: Imagine that a local cable station was invaded by otherdimensional creatures at the stroke of midnight. That's Video Vortex. Each month, this series presents a mystery transmission that's culled from the outer limits of home video history – from essential underground films to surreal docs, from tokusatsu battle-parties to outsider experiments. So warm up the cathode tubes, dim the lights, and let your senses intermingle with the glow.

verdict.reason: Skip it unless you're already committed to the Video Vortex series or have a taste for deep-cut oddities from home video history. At 77 minutes, it's a low-stakes gamble, but the appeal depends entirely on what this month's transmission actually contains.
